identity.title: A Random Matrix Perspective on the Consistency of Diffusion Models

problem.claim: Explain why diffusion models trained on non-overlapping data subsets can produce similar outputs from the same noise seed, and quantify cross-split consistency.

contributions.claim: Develops an RMT framework for quantifying finite-data effects on the learned denoiser and sampling map in linear diffusion models.
Extends deterministic-equivalence tools to fractional matrix powers to analyze full sampling trajectories.
Links data spectral properties to generative-output stability as a baseline for reproducibility in diffusion training.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present an RMT treatment that explains diffusion consistency through shared Gaussian statistics and analyzes both expectations, fluctuations, and sampling trajectories.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that shared Gaussian statistics across data splits predict much of the generated imagery.
The authors report that the theory sharply predicts linear diffusion-model behavior and validate those predictions on UNet and DiT models in their non-memorization regime.
The authors report variance formulas identifying anisotropy, input inhomogeneity, and dataset size as factors governing cross-split disagreement.

narrative_sequence.summary: Non-overlapping training subsets can yield strikingly similar outputs under the same noise seed.
The authors attribute much of this consistency to shared Gaussian statistics across splits.
An RMT framework quantifies finite-dataset effects, including expectation renormalization and fluctuation sources.
Fractional matrix-power tools cover sampling trajectories, and predictions are tested on UNet and DiT models outside memorization.
The resulting account is positioned as a reproducibility baseline linking data spectra to output stability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates expected behavior from disagreement: limited data renormalizes effective noise and overshrinks low-variance directions, while variance depends on anisotropy, input inhomogeneity, and dataset size.

lessons.interpretation: A useful analysis can make reproducibility claims more diagnostic by distinguishing systematic bias from split-to-split fluctuations.
lessons.application: Report separate mechanisms for mean drift and variance, then map each to measurable data or model properties.
lessons.exception: This decomposition may not transfer directly beyond the stated linear setting or the non-memorization regime.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the quantitative prediction errors or validation metrics for UNet and DiT.
The scope and assumptions of the linear theory, including dataset and noise conditions, are not detailed.
It is unclear how much of the generated-image similarity is explained quantitatively by the shared Gaussian statistics.
